blocks.value:
# Project ends, product evolves

Picture two requests that could land on your desk: the website for an event happening in November, and the delivery app a company wants to keep running for the next ten years. The first is a PROJECT: a temporary effort, with a beginning, middle, and end, an agreed scope, and a date when it is over. The second is a PRODUCT: something alive, that solves a recurring problem for a group of people and evolves as long as that problem exists.

The difference looks bureaucratic, but it changes everything. A project is measured by delivery: met the scope, deadline, and budget, success. A product is measured by outcome: someone uses it, the use solves the problem, the business sustains itself with it. The event website can be perfect and never touched again. The launched delivery app is just the beginning: user behavior will reveal what works, and the team will adjust, cut, and rebuild for years.

Whoever treats product as a project delivers, celebrates, and disbands the team. Three months later, the app is outdated, competitors have moved, and nobody is left to learn from what users are doing inside it.

[["Aspect","Project","Product"],["End","Defined delivery date","Evolves as long as the problem exists"],["Success","Scope, deadline, and budget","Outcome for the user and the business"],["Scope","Closed at the start","A bet revised with feedback"],["Team","Disbanded at delivery","Stays to learn and adjust"],["Key question","Did we deliver what was agreed?","Are we solving the problem?"]]
A project ends when it delivers. A product begins when it delivers: that is when the user shows up and your hypotheses get tested.

## Why the mindset changes everything

Imagine a digital bank that commissions a 'three-step sign-up' from a team. The team delivers on time, on budget, pixel perfect. In project logic, party. Then the data arrives: 70% of people abandon at step two. In product logic, that is not success, it is the start of the work: why do they abandon? What did we ask for too early? What can be cut?

This mindset changes how you plan. The roadmap stops being a contract ('in March we deliver X') and becomes a sequence of bets ('we believe X reduces abandonment; if it does not, we change the plan'). It changes how you measure: less 'quarterly deliveries', more 'what changed in the behavior of those who use it'. And it changes how the company invests: product asks for a stable team, because the knowledge about the user lives in the people who follow the day to day.

Throughout this trail, that is the lens. You will see roles, teams, users, business, and communication, always with the same underlying question: is this making the product produce results, or just producing beautiful deliveries to watch in a report?

blocks.value:
# A shipped feature is not value

At the end of the quarter, the team celebrates: twelve features shipped, release notes packed, a beautiful demo for the board. Then someone opens the dashboard: retention flat, conversion flat, support receiving the same tickets as always. Lots of OUTPUT, no OUTCOME.

Output is what the team produces: screens, features, releases, lines of code. Outcome is the change that causes in the world: the user who starts solving the problem faster, the customer who stops canceling, the operation that stops depending on a spreadsheet. Output is under your direct control; outcome is the consequence you chase and that the world needs to confirm.

An example to make it stick. In a digital bank app, 'letting users customize the virtual card color' is output. The intended outcome might be 'more people activate the card and start using it as their main one'. If the customization ships and activation does not move, there was delivery without value. If activation rises with no new feature at all, for example just reordering the home screen, there was value with very little delivery. The scoreboard is the second one, not the first.

[["Situation","Output","Outcome sought"],["E-commerce with poor search","New search filter","More people find and buy"],["Support flooded with tickets","In-app help center","Fewer repeated tickets"],["Sign-up with abandonment","Flow cut to 2 steps","More accounts reach the end"],["Deliveries running late","Tracking dashboard","Less anxiety and cancellation"]]
Nobody wakes up wanting to use your feature. People want progress in their lives; the feature is just the means of transportation.

## How to recognize each one day to day

The test is one question: 'if this works, what changes in the behavior of whoever uses it?'. If the answer describes the delivery ('we will have chat in the app'), you are talking about output. If it describes an observable change ('the customer resolves in minutes what today takes hours'), it is outcome.

The danger of output is that it is comfortable: it is visible, photographable, fits in a report. From there comes delivery theater: teams very busy, velocity charts rising, and the business stuck in the same place. The way out is not stopping delivery; it is tying each delivery to an expected outcome BEFORE building, and coming back to check whether the bridge happened after launch.

Watch out for the other extreme: outcome without output does not exist either. Results come from delivery that worked; a PM who only talks metrics and does not help the team ship anything does not move the scoreboard either. The practical rule you take from this lesson: goals written as outcomes, daily work organized as outputs, and the honesty to check the connection between the two every month.

blocks.value:
# Four phases, four different games

Products have a lifecycle, and each phase is a game with its own rules. In INTRODUCTION, the product has just been born and is still looking for its fit: few users, much uncertainty, abrupt direction changes are normal and even healthy. In GROWTH, the fit has appeared and demand pulls: the challenge becomes scaling without breaking, repeating what works, opening channels. In MATURITY, growth slows: the fight becomes efficiency, margin, and defending the position against competitors. In DECLINE, usage falls consistently: the honest decision is to reinvent, harvest what is left, or shut down with dignity.

Think of an urban rideshare app. Early on, the team changes the product every week chasing the format that makes driver and rider come back. Once it finds it, the game becomes neighborhood coverage and wait time. Years later, with a contested market, it becomes price, efficiency, and a loyalty program. If a new mode takes its place, it becomes a portfolio decision. Same product, four completely different jobs, and the team that does not notice the shift plays the wrong game.

[["Phase","Typical sign","Team focus"],["Introduction","Few users, much uncertainty","Learn fast and find the fit"],["Growth","Demand pulling, channels opening","Scale without breaking what works"],["Maturity","Slow growth, margin in focus","Efficiency, retention, and defense"],["Decline","Consistent usage drop","Reinvent, harvest, or shut down"]]
Managing a mature product as if it were new burns money; managing a new product as if it were mature kills discovery. Getting the phase wrong gets everything after it wrong.

## What the team does differently in each phase

In introduction, the virtue is throwing away without mercy: the goal is to learn, so features, screens, and even the target audience can change. Scale metrics (revenue, market share) say little; what matters is signal of value: does anyone come back? Recommend? Miss it when the app goes down?

In growth, the virtue flips: discipline to NOT break what works. Experiments continue, but protecting the core that sustains demand. Operation and support bottlenecks appear, the team grows, and much of the work becomes coordinating new people.

In maturity, compound optimization: 2% improvements that add up, new segments for the same engine, cutting the cost to serve. It is the phase where accumulated debt charges interest, and where many teams err out of boredom: they invent features nobody asked for just to feel motion.

In decline, honesty: recognize the fall early, understand whether it is the product's or the whole category's, and decide with data. Migrating users with respect is also product work. Knowing which phase your product is in is the first diagnosis of any decision.

# B2C, B2B, marketplace, platform, and internal

Saying 'I work with product' is like saying 'I work with sports': the game changes completely depending on the type. In B2C (direct to consumer, like a delivery or streaming app), you deal with volume: millions of users, fast and emotional usage decisions, short experiment cycles. In B2B (companies selling to companies, like a management system for restaurants), there are few high-value customers, a long sales cycle, and a central trap: whoever USES the product is rarely whoever SIGNS the contract.

A marketplace connects two sides, sellers and buyers, like a real-world Mercado Livre, and inherits the chicken-and-egg problem: without supply there is no demand, without demand there is no supply. Platform and API have the developer as user: documentation is the interface, and stability is worth more than novelty. Internal product serves the company itself: the user is captive, which tempts people into justifying a bad experience, and success is measured in operation productivity, not direct revenue.

[["Type","Who decides to use","Central challenge"],["B2C","The user themselves","Win attention and create habit at scale"],["B2B","A buyer who is not the user","Serve whoever uses and whoever signs at once"],["Marketplace","Two sides at once","Balance supply and demand"],["Platform/API","Developers","Stability, documentation, and trust"],["Internal","The company imposes","Keep quality even with a captive user"]]
In B2B, whoever suffers with the product is rarely whoever signs the contract. Confusing the two is the origin of much hated software.

## What changes for those building product

The product type defines your tools. In B2C, quantitative data rules: with millions of users, A/B tests and funnels are the day to day, and every second of friction matters. In B2B, you know customers by name: research is deep conversation, the roadmap suffers pressure from contracts ('the big client asked'), and saying no takes political game. In a marketplace, every decision needs to be thought through twice, once per side: lowering the commission pleases sellers and may worsen the service for buyers.

In a platform, your user reads the changelog: breaking compatibility is the capital sin, and the success metric includes the success of OTHER products built on top of yours. In internal product, the temptation is skipping research ('we already know what operations need'); the best teams treat colleagues as customers, with onboarding, metrics, and a real roadmap.

No type is superior. But knowing which one is yours changes what you measure, how you research, and with whom you negotiate. In 2026 job postings, the distinction shows up right in the title: marketplace PM, platform PM, B2B PM.

lessons.title: Where product lives in the company

blocks.value:
# The function that connects

Product does not build, design, sell, or support: product CONNECTS. The value of the role is making engineering, design, marketing, sales, and support pull in the same direction, each area with its own lens. With ENGINEERING, the conversation is feasibility and cost: what can be built, in how long, with which risks. With DESIGN, it is desirability and usability: do people understand, manage, and want to use it. Those two, together with product, form the trio you will unpack in module 3.

With MARKETING, the conversation is positioning and acquisition: what story the market will hear, through which channel, and whether the product delivers the campaign's promise. With SALES, it is promise and contract: what was sold must exist, and what exists must be sellable; when sales promises what does not exist, the product becomes a hostage of improvisation. With SUPPORT, it is the naked truth: no research reveals as much about the product as the ticket queue on any random Monday. People working in product circulate among these five conversations every day.

[["Area","What it brings","Typical conversation with product"],["Engineering","Technical feasibility and cost","What to build and at what price"],["Design","Usability and desire","Does the user understand and want this?"],["Marketing","Positioning and acquisition","What promise will we make to the market?"],["Sales","Revenue and contracts","Does what was promised exist?"],["Support","The real day-to-day pain","What generates the most tickets today?"]]
Support knows before everyone else when the product got worse. A product team that does not read tickets is doing research with closed eyes.

## Influence without authority

Here is the truth that knocks many people down in their first week: product is nobody's boss. Engineering answers to an engineering manager, design to a design manager, marketing to another. You coordinate without commanding, and your currency is context: whoever understands the problem, the user, and the business can align people who owe you nothing.

A classic failure scenario: the team prepares a launch for two months and tells marketing the day before. Result: improvised campaign, support caught by surprise, sales learning the news from the customer. The technically perfect launch becomes a commercial failure. The lesson is not 'have more meetings'; it is: the areas that will carry your product need to come in early enough to influence, not just to execute.

In practice, product lives on translation: turning a business goal into a problem for the team, support data into a priority, a technical constraint into an honest conversation with the board. If you like being right alone, the role hurts. If you like making a system of people work, it is the best place in the company to be.

lessons.title: Product Manager: owner of the problem

blocks.value:
# Owner of the problem, not of the backlog

Ask ten people what a Product Manager does and you get ten answers, almost all wrong. The definition that carries this trail: the PM is the OWNER OF THE PROBLEM. They answer for making sure the team is solving something that matters to the user and the business, and that the chosen solution has a real chance of working. The backlog, the task board, and the schedule are consequences; the problem is the origin.

The real day to day is less glamorous than LinkedIn suggests: talking with users and stakeholders, writing (a lot), analyzing data to understand what is happening, prioritizing with incomplete information, and aligning people who disagree. The decision is rarely 'which feature is genius'; it is almost always 'given what we know today, which problem do we attack first and what do we stop doing'.

Note the verb: deciding with incomplete information. If you wait for certainty to act, product will be uncomfortable. The professional PM builds as much context as possible in the available time, decides, communicates the why, and takes responsibility for correcting course when new data arrives.

[["Myth","Reality"],["PM is the product's mini-CEO","PM influences without authority; a CEO commands"],["PM is the team's boss","Engineering and design have their own managers"],["PM is a project manager","Deadline is the means; the end is outcome in usage"],["PM defines everything alone","Decides together with the trio and with data"],["PM needs to code","Needs to talk technically, not to code"]]
The PM is not the team's boss. They are the person making sure the team is spending its life solving a problem worth solving.

## What the PM is NOT

Three deviations appear in every company. The PROJECT MANAGER IN DISGUISE: lives on schedules, chases status, measures success by on-time delivery. Useful? Sometimes. But if nobody is watching over which problem to solve, the team delivers the wrong thing fast. The BACKLOG SECRETARY: writes down stakeholder requests, turns them into tickets, and passes them to the team, with no filter or criteria. Becomes a feature waiter, and the product becomes the sum of requests from whoever shouts loudest. And the MINI-CEO: believes the myth, tries to command, and discovers the hard way that nobody owes them obedience.

The antidote for all three is the same: go back to the problem. When someone asks for a feature, ask what problem it solves and for whom. When pressed for a deadline, show the outcome the date buys or sacrifices. When feeling the urge to command, remember your strength is the context you carry, not the title. In the next modules you will see the tools; none of them work without this problem-owner posture.

# From Scrum role to market job title

Product Owner was born inside Scrum: it is the role responsible for maximizing the value of the team's work, owner of the Product Backlog, the one who orders items and accepts (or not) what was built. In the manual, PO is not a career position; it is a function within the framework, and a person holding the Product Manager title could perform it.

The Brazilian market, however, turned the title into a job, and in 2026 the confusion remains strong in job postings. In the most common usage here, PO describes someone closer to delivery: refines the backlog with the team, writes user stories, answers business-rule questions, validates delivery. PM describes someone closer to strategy: discovers problems, talks with the market, defines direction and metrics. In many companies the two roles coexist in layers; in others, it is the same person with whatever title HR picked that year.

The split 'PM owns the why and the what, PO owns the how and the when with the team' is an honest summary of Brazilian usage, as long as you remember: it is a snapshot of the market, not a law.

USER STORY (classic format)

As a customer who received the wrong order,
I want to request a refund directly in the app,
so I can resolve it without calling support.

Acceptance criteria:
- Eligible order shows a 'Request refund' button
- Customer picks a reason from a list (wrong, missing, damaged item)
- Confirmation shows the deadline and amount to refund
- Out-of-policy cases go to manual review with a clear notice

[["Dimension","PO (common use in Brazil)","PM"],["Horizon","Sprint and quarter","Quarter and year"],["Focus","Refine, detail, accept","Discover, prioritize, measure"],["Most frequent conversation","Development team","Users and stakeholders"],["Typical question","Is this ready to go in?","Is this worth doing?"]]
In an interview, ignore the title and ask about the scope: who discovers the problem, who decides the priority, who talks with the user. The answer tells you what the job really is.

## How to navigate the titles without getting lost

In practice, what matters is the role's REAL SCOPE, and it varies by company, not by title. There are POs in Brazil doing top-level discovery and strategy, and PMs who spend the whole day writing tickets. So when evaluating a job or presenting yourself, describe what you DO: 'I discovered problem X by talking to N customers, prioritized it against Y, and the outcome was Z'. That communicates seniority in any vocabulary.

A day-to-day tool associated with the PO role deserves attention: the user story. The 'as a [persona], I want [action], so that [benefit]' format is not bureaucracy; it is a reminder that every delivery has a user and an expected value. The most neglected part is the 'so that': without the explicit benefit, the team has no way to question the solution or propose a better path. A good story fits in a conversation; acceptance criteria delimit what 'done' means. If the story becomes a ten-page contract, the spirit was lost along the way.

lessons.title: Product Analyst and APM: the entry door

blocks.value:
# Where the career begins

Almost nobody enters product directly as a PM, and that is fine. The two most common doors have names: PRODUCT ANALYST and APM (Associate Product Manager). The Product Analyst is the team's data and evidence arm: builds dashboards, investigates why a metric fell, prepares analyses that support prioritization decisions, helps design and read experiments, organizes user feedback. They are the one turning 'I think' into 'the data suggests'.

The APM is the same destination by another road: structured training programs, with rotation across teams, mentoring from senior PMs, and growing responsibility. In 2026 Brazil these programs are still rare (a few big techs keep theirs), so the Analyst route, or a junior PO, remains the most realistic for most people.

What the two roles have in common: you learn the craft next to people who already decide, with protected scope. What changes the game is how you use that period: you can spend two years pulling data for others, or use every analysis as a decision rehearsal.

[["Analyst activity","Executor version","Version that becomes a step"],["Dashboard","Delivers the requested panel","Points out what the panel reveals and suggests action"],["Drop analysis","Describes the drop","Raises hypotheses and proposes the next step"],["User feedback","Compiles into a spreadsheet","Synthesizes patterns and connects to the roadmap"],["Experiment","Calculates the result","Recommends a decision based on the result"]]
The distance between Analyst and PM is measured in one sentence: do you end the analysis with a number or with a recommendation?

## How the role grows

The progression has a clear ladder: from ANALYSIS (what happened) to RECOMMENDATION (what we should do), and from recommendation to DECISION (owning a problem and answering for it). Each step is a habit you practice before earning the title. An Analyst who delivers analysis with a written recommendation is doing a PM internship in public; when an internal opening appears, the track record already exists.

The most effective move, and the most repeated advice from hiring managers: ask to own a SMALL problem end to end. A password-recovery flow, the FAQ page, an internal report nobody loves. Small enough not to scare anyone, complete enough for you to exercise the whole cycle: understand the problem, propose, prioritize, follow the delivery, measure, and tell the story of the result.

The role's trap is comfort on the other side: becoming the team's 'pet SQL', ever faster at pulling data and ever further from decisions. If all your quarter's deliverables were consumed by someone else who decided in your place, it is time to renegotiate the scope.

# The cast around the product

Four roles orbit the product team and cause constant confusion. The SCRUM MASTER (or Agile Coach) takes care of the PROCESS: facilitates ceremonies, removes impediments, helps the team work better; does not decide what to build. The PRODUCT DESIGNER takes care of the EXPERIENCE: researches users, explores solutions, designs flows and screens; in mature companies they join discovery from day one, they do not receive 'the request to design' at the end.

The PRODUCT MARKETING MANAGER (PMM) takes care of the BRIDGE TO THE MARKET: positioning, message, launch, sales enablement. If the PM guarantees the product solves the problem, the PMM guarantees the market hears about it in the right terms. And the BUSINESS ANALYST (BA), a strong role in banks and traditional companies, maps processes and requirements, especially where a new system touches an old system and regulatory rules.

None of these boundaries are clean in real life. Is user research the designer's or the PM's? Is the launch message the PMM's or the PM's? The honest answer: it depends on the company, the moment, and the people.

[["Role","Focus","Common overlap with the PM"],["Scrum Master / Agile Coach","Process and impediments","Rituals and team health"],["Product Designer","Research and experience","Discovery and user contact"],["Product Marketing (PMM)","Positioning and launch","Product message and narrative"],["Business Analyst","Processes and requirements","Detailing business rules"]]
Role overlap is not an org-chart defect, it is the nature of creative work. The defect is pretending it does not exist and leaving the boundary to be discovered in a crisis.

## Boundaries are negotiated, not memorized

The wrong question is 'whose task is this according to the manual'. The right one: 'on this team, for this work, who takes what?'. Mature teams make that agreement explicit. A concrete example: at a launch, PM and PMM sit down and split it: the PM writes the internal document with the problem, solution, and metrics; the PMM writes the external narrative and validates it with close customers; both review each other's material. Twenty minutes of conversation save weeks of resentment.

Two signs of an unresolved boundary for you to recognize: DUPLICATED WORK (two people discover late they did the same thing) and NO MAN'S LAND (everyone thought it was the other's, and the launch shipped without support material). When you notice either, the fix is not escalating to the boss: it is pulling the explicit agreement back out.

With the Scrum Master, the healthy partnership is clear: they protect the HOW of work, you answer for the WHAT and the WHY. When the process becomes an end in itself, ceremony after ceremony, it is the PM's role to bring the conversation back to the outcome.

# Steps of scope, not of status

The market's most common ladder: APM or Product Analyst, PM, Senior PM, GPM or Product Lead, Head of Product or CPO. The classic mistake is reading this sequence as a status ladder, each step commanding the previous. The right reading is SCOPE AND AMBIGUITY: what grows at each step is the size of the problem you solve and how much nobody knows the answer before you.

On the first step, you execute with supervision: bounded problems, decisions reviewed by someone more experienced. As a PM, you become owner of a product or area: you decide with autonomy within a given direction. As a SENIOR, problems arrive with no statement: 'our engagement looks weird' instead of 'improve onboarding'; you define the problem before solving it, influence beyond your team, and develop juniors without holding a management title.

At the GPM or Lead step the nature of the work truly changes: you start multiplying THROUGH OTHER PMs. Less deciding the product, more developing who decides. It is management, with everything it charges: hard feedback, hiring, other people's careers.

[["Step","Typical scope","What changes"],["APM / Analyst","Bounded problems","Executes with supervision and learns the craft"],["PM","One product or area","Decides with autonomy within the direction"],["Senior PM","Problems with no statement","Defines the problem and influences beyond the team"],["GPM / Lead","Several teams","Multiplies through other PMs: management"],["Head / CPO","Portfolio and organization","Product strategy, structure, and culture"]]
Climbing the product career is trading bigger problems for less certainty: the more senior, the less someone tells you what to do, and the more people expect you to know.

## Two tracks and one honest criterion

At the top, Head and CPO work on another layer: portfolio (which bets the company makes), organization (how teams split), and culture (how decisions are made here). They are far from each screen's detail, and that distance is the price of the scope.

Two practical warnings. First: management is NOT the only path. An excellent senior PM who does not want to manage people can keep growing as an individual contributor, attacking the company's thorniest problems; forcing every senior into management produces bad managers and loses great problem solvers. If the company does not offer that track, that is information about the company.

Second: the mature promotion criterion is DEMONSTRATED IMPACT AT THE NEXT SCOPE, not tenure. 'I have been here two years' is not an argument; 'I took on an ambiguous problem, defined it, solved it, and here is the result' is. This also works the other way: if you have been operating at the next step for a year and the company does not recognize it, the 2026 market does. Build the track record in writing; it is your promotion case, here or elsewhere.

# Three chairs in the same decision

Every product team that works has a small decision core: product, design, and engineering. It is the TRIO. Each chair arrives with a different question, and it is the crossing of them that produces good decisions. Product asks whether it is worth it: the problem matters to whoever uses it and the outcome matters to the business. Design asks whether people can and want to: does the flow make sense, is the language clear, does the effort fit the life of whoever is on the other side. Engineering asks whether it can be built and at what price: what is expensive, what is risky, what already exists ready, and what will charge maintenance for years.

The opposite of the trio is the internal waterfall, more common than admitted: the PM writes a document with the solution ready, hands it to design to 'make it pretty', and design delivers screens for engineering to 'implement'. Each handoff loses context, and the risk only appears at the end, when changing is expensive. It is telephone game with a deadline.

In the trio, all three enter the problem definition TOGETHER. Design can show the pain is elsewhere; engineering can offer a path ten times cheaper nobody had imagined. No document replaces this conversation.

[["Chair","Question it brings","Risk it helps avoid"],["Product","Is it worth solving this now?","Building something that does not matter"],["Design","Does the person understand and manage?","A solution usable only by its creators"],["Engineering","Can it be built, at what cost?","Blown deadlines and expensive maintenance"],["Trio together","Which problem do we attack first?","Deciding with half the context"]]
A document does not replace a conversation. When design and engineering receive the decision ready-made, the team loses the two best chances to find a better path.

## Collaborative decision is not decision by consensus

Trio does not mean voting on everything or blocking until everyone agrees. It means deciding with the THREE LENSES at the table, with clear responsibilities: product answers for the problem and the priority, design answers for the experience, engineering answers for the technical solution and feasibility. When there is a tie, someone decides and owns it. The healthy agreement is recording the decision with the why, so it is not re-discussed every week.

A common scenario at a fintech: the team needs to reduce account-opening abandonment. In the waterfall, the PM arrives with 'let's remove two form fields'. In the trio, the designer brings recordings showing abandonment concentrates on the document photo, and the engineer remembers there is already a contracted service that validates documents with much less friction. The final decision belongs to no one alone, and it is better than any of the three initial ones.

Signs of a healthy trio: all three people explain the problem in the same words; engineering participates before the scope closes; design talks with users alongside the PM. If you are the only one who knows why the team is doing that, there is no trio, there is handoff.

# By feature, by journey, or by platform

How the company splits teams defines what it can build without everything becoming a meeting. Three cuts appear almost always. By FEATURE: each team owns a piece of the product, like search, checkout, or notifications. Easy to set up, and it tends to produce teams that ship pieces without seeing the whole outcome. By JOURNEY: the team owns a user path end to end, like 'first purchase' or 'renewal', with a metric that is its own. It gives more autonomy and forces the team to look at the problem, not the screen. By PLATFORM: teams serving other teams, like auth, payments, or data, whose customers are internal and whose success is measured in the productivity of whoever depends on them.

No cut is neutral. What sits at the boundary between two teams is what delays. So the question when designing teams is not 'which model is in fashion', but which problems need to be solved without depending on agreement between five teams.

In Brazil, the term SQUAD became a synonym for team, copied from models published by big companies without the context that made them work. Swapping 'team' for 'squad' changes nothing; changing who decides does.

[["Cut","Example team","Strength","Weakness"],["By feature","Search team","Focus and technical domain","Loses the end-to-end outcome"],["By journey","First-purchase team","Own metric and autonomy","Disputes screens with other teams"],["By platform","Payments team","Scale and internal reuse","Far from the end user"],["By segment","Big-merchant team","Knows the customer deeply","Duplicates effort across segments"]]
An empowered team receives a problem and answers for an outcome. A feature team receives a list and answers for dates. The org chart can be the same; the work is not.

## Empowered teams and feature teams

Marty Cagan popularized two terms that today work as market vocabulary. The FEATURE TEAM receives a list of things to build and is measured by delivering that list. The EMPOWERED TEAM receives a problem, with an outcome metric and freedom to choose the solution, and is measured by the outcome.

The difference does not show up in the org chart, it shows up in Monday's conversation. If leadership arrives with 'we need to launch the coupon by June', it is a feature team. If it arrives with 'repurchase dropped eight points, what do you propose?', it is an empowered team. Real autonomy requires three things the company must grant: shared business context, direct access to users and data, and tolerance for experiments that did not work.

An honest warning for those starting out: a good part of the 2026 openings are on teams closer to the feature team, and that does not invalidate your work. You can pull autonomy bit by bit: delivering the request along with a reading of the problem, proposing a cheaper alternative with data in hand, turning 'do X' into 'the goal is Y, and X is one hypothesis'. Autonomy is rarely granted in a block; it is earned in small decisions that worked.

# Meetings are cost, rituals are investment

Every recurring meeting is a fixed cost paid in hours of expensive people. A ritual only justifies itself when it produces something asynchronous conversation would not: a decision, a hard alignment, a course correction. The rest is inherited habit.

Three rituals usually pay their own price. The TRIO SYNC, short and frequent, is where product, design, and engineering look at what is in flight, what is stuck, and what needs deciding this week. It keeps discovery and delivery from running on separate tracks. The STAKEHOLDER REVIEW shows what was done, what was learned, and what changes in the plan; well run, it replaces dozens of one-off status messages. And the METRIC RITUAL, monthly, is where the team opens the numbers of what it launched and asks whether the bet worked.

Notice the pattern: all three end with something. A ritual that ends only with 'everyone updated' is competing with a document, and it will lose. The question sustaining any recurring meeting is simple: if we cancel it for a month, what breaks?

[["Ritual","What it is for","Sign it became theater"],["Trio sync","Decide what blocks the week","Becomes an individual status report"],["Stakeholder review","Show learning and adjust","Becomes a demo to impress a director"],["Metric ritual","See if the bet worked","Nobody asks what to do now"],["Planning","Agree on the period's focus","Arrives with everything decided from outside"]]
If a ritual could be replaced by a well-written document, it should be replaced by a well-written document.

## The minimum that works

Beginner teams tend toward two extremes. The first is the packed calendar: ceremony every day, no gaps in the schedule, and no block of focused work left. The second is the total absence of ritual, which looks like freedom until the day two people discover they built incompatible things.

The practical path is starting with the minimum and adding only when it hurts. A short trio sync, an alignment conversation with stakeholders at the cycle's rhythm, and a moment to look at numbers. Everything else must justify its own existence. And rituals should be reviewed: every quarter, it is worth asking team by team which meetings still earn their keep and which became habit.

Two rules that improve any ritual, at no cost. First: every recurring meeting has an owner, a written purpose, and an expected output; without that, it does not enter the calendar. Second: a decision made in a meeting becomes text the same day, in the place where the team looks for information. Whoever missed it does not need to ask, and whoever was there does not need to remember from memory three weeks later. A ritual without a record produces the same discussion again in fifteen days.

# Technical debt is a business conversation

Technical debt is the future cost of a shortcut taken today. Sometimes the shortcut is the right decision: shipping fast to test a hypothesis is worth more than the perfect architecture of a product nobody wants. The problem is not taking on debt, it is pretending it does not exist and paying interest in silence, in the form of recurring bugs, ever-slower deliveries, and a demotivated team.

The PM does not need to assess code quality, but needs to be able to talk about cost and risk. When engineering says 'we need to refactor the payments module', the useful question is not 'is this really necessary?', it is 'what happens to the business if we do not do it, and when?'. The answer turns a technical request into a product decision: more incidents at sales peak, overloaded support, new features that start costing double.

The pattern that works is reserving capacity explicitly, agreed with the team, instead of promising 'we'll fix it later'. Later never arrives, because there is always something more urgent to put in its place.

[["Technical request","Translation for the business","Decision that becomes clear"],["Refactor checkout","Every change costs double today","Invest now or pay more later"],["Replace the payments queue","Peak incidents break payouts","Take the risk or reduce it now"],["Cover module tests","Regression reaches the customer","Accept rework or prevent"],["Update dependency","Open security failure","Handle it before or explain after"]]

TECH DEBT ITEM WRITTEN FOR DECISION

Title: Manual reprocessing in the payments queue
Symptom today: 3 incidents this quarter, 40h of manual operation
Risk if nothing changes: sales peak breaks merchant payouts
Estimated cost: 2 team-weeks, with a wide error margin
Expected gain: fewer incidents, less support, base for installments
Decision requested: go now, go after the launch, or stay on record
An estimate is not a promise, it is the team's best reading of uncertainty today. Charging for an estimate as if it were a contract teaches the team to lie with padding.

## Estimates, uncertainty, and trust

An estimate is a forecast under uncertainty, and uncertainty shrinks as the team learns. A vague request, with unknown integrations, has a huge error margin; the same request after a two-day investigation becomes much more predictable. So the mature question is not 'how long does it take?', but 'what would you need to know to have more confidence in this estimate?'.

The cycle that destroys trust is well known. The PM pressures for a date, the team guesses low to please, the deadline blows, quality drops, and the next guess comes inflated for self-protection. The way out is changing the conversation's currency: deadline with a range and confidence level, negotiable scope, and the honesty to tell the board that a single date with no margin is fiction.

Trust is built with repeated behavior. Not changing priority mid-cycle without talking, defending the team when external pressure arrives, explaining the why of every decision, and admitting when you got the bet wrong. Engineering that trusts the PM brings problems early. Engineering that does not trust hides the problem until it becomes a crisis.

# Shared research, shared decision

The most common mistake a junior PM makes with design is treating the pair as a production line: the PM brings the problem already solved, design makes it presentable. That wastes the partnership's most valuable part. A product designer is not the person who picks colors; it is the person who investigates how people think, tests paths, and turns a confusing problem into a flow someone can walk without a manual.

The practice that changes this game is SHARED RESEARCH. Instead of splitting 'design does interviews, PM reads the report', both watch the same user conversations, each with their own lens. The designer notices the hesitation in front of a screen; the PM notices the sentence revealing how much that costs the person's business. When both heard the same thing, the discussion about what to do gets short, because the evidence is shared.

The practical rule is simple: the PM does not design, but participates. Participating means coming in early, bringing business constraints before rather than after, and discussing alternatives while they are still a cheap sketch to throw away.

[["Situation","PM who gets in the way","PM who adds"],["Start of the problem","Arrives with the screen done","Arrives with the problem and the outcome"],["Research","Waits for the final report","Watches the sessions with design"],["Work critique","Says they did not like the look","Points out goal, risk, and evidence"],["Tight deadline","Cuts research entirely","Reduces the scope of what will be tested"]]
Useful design feedback does not talk about taste, it talks about the goal: what does this screen need the person to understand, and what in the current proposal gets in the way.

## How to critique design without becoming a decorator

Design critique is a learnable skill. The useless version sounds like: 'not feeling it', 'I think it looks better in blue', 'make it like the competitor's'. The useful version separates three things: GOAL (what this screen needs the person to understand or do), OBSERVATION (what in the proposal may hinder that goal), and OPEN QUESTION (what you did not understand and want explained). Whoever critiques this way does not invade the other's craft, and still helps the decision.

Avoid the opposite extreme too, the PM who stays silent. Polite silence before launch becomes disapproval after, and redoing at the end is expensive for everyone. Business constraints, legal limits, and risk rules need to appear in the sketch, not on the eve.

One sign of a healthy partnership: on a well-tuned team, it is hard to tell whose idea it was. The best decisions are usually born mid-conversation, when someone joins the pain observed in research with the technical constraint and someone else completes it with the business goal. If you feel you need to beat the designer in a discussion, the problem is no longer the screen.

# The trap of the enchanting solution

An idea arrives ready and brilliant: 'we need an AI assistant inside the app'. It is seductive, fits in a sentence, makes a good presentation. And that is exactly where the trap lives: when someone falls in love with a solution, they start hunting for a problem to justify it. The team builds, launches, and discovers the real pain was another one, more boring and less photogenic.

Product works in the PROBLEM SPACE before entering the solution space. In the problem space you describe who suffers, in what situation, how often, and how much it costs today. In the solution space you choose how to attack. Skipping the first is like buying medicine before the diagnosis: sometimes it works, and you never know why.

This does not mean turning every request into an interrogation. When the solution is cheap, reversible, and the problem is evident, do it and move on. The rigor must be proportional to the cost: the more expensive and harder to undo, the more it is worth investigating the problem before writing the first line of code.

[["Incoming request","Question that reveals","Problem that may be behind it"],["I want an AI chat","What made you think of this now?","Support is slow to answer simple questions"],["We need an app","Who will use it, and when?","The site works poorly on mobile"],["Build a new report","What decision does this report support?","Nobody trusts the current numbers"],["Copy the competitor's feature","What outcome do we expect?","Fear of losing clients with no evidence"]]
Every feature request carries a hidden problem and a guessed solution. Your job is separating the two before the team builds the guess.

## How to reframe a request without being annoying

Reframing starts with curiosity, not resistance. Instead of 'why do you want this?', which sounds like an interrogation, it works better to ask what happened recently that led to the request, who felt the pain, and what those people do today to work around it. The hack is gold: when someone keeps a parallel spreadsheet, exports a report and redoes the math by hand, the problem is screaming right there.

After understanding, write the problem in one short sentence anyone on the team can repeat. A helpful format: WHO, in WHAT SITUATION, cannot do WHAT, and therefore pays WHAT PRICE. For example: 'the small merchant, when closing the month, cannot check payouts and spends two hours in the spreadsheet, with the risk of charging wrong'.

That statement changes the whole conversation. With it, several solutions can be compared, including ones nobody had imagined, and success stops being 'we shipped the chat' and becomes 'the merchant closes the month in minutes'. Whoever writes the problem well has already won half the priority discussion.

lessons.title: Jobs To Be Done and the milkshake job

blocks.value:
# People hire products to do a job

The story became a classic in the product world. A fast-food chain wanted to sell more milkshakes and did the usual: asked customers which flavor, texture, and price profile would please most. It adjusted the product to the answers and sales did not move. A research team, connected to Clayton Christensen's work, decided to look another way and started observing WHEN purchases happened.

The discovery: a huge slice of the milkshakes was bought early in the morning, by people alone, who took the drink in the car. They did not want dessert. They were hiring the milkshake for a very specific job: fill a long, boring commute and hold hunger until lunch. In that job, the competitors were not other milkshakes; they were the banana, the donut, and the cereal bar.

That is the central idea of JOBS TO BE DONE. People do not buy products, they hire solutions to make progress in their lives. Understanding the job explains choices demographics never would.

[["Customer's job","Typical situation","Real competitors"],["Fill the commute and hold hunger","Long morning traffic","Banana, donut, cereal bar"],["Prove the month closed right","Merchant's month-end","Parallel spreadsheet and accountant"],["Not embarrass myself in the meeting","Presentation to the board","A colleague's slides and improvising"],["Kill time in line","A ten-minute wait","Social network, game, news"]]
Nobody wants a drill, everyone wants the hole in the wall. And sometimes not even the hole: they want the shelf in place with no mess and no headache.

## Progress, not demographics

JTBD's most useful shift is this: CIRCUMSTANCE explains more than PROFILE. Two people with the same age, income, and city hire different products depending on the moment; the same person hires different solutions on Monday morning and Friday night. So the job usually has three layers: the functional (what needs to be done), the emotional (how the person wants to feel), and the social (how they want to be seen by others).

In practice, you reach the job by interviewing about the CONCRETE PAST, never about the hypothetical future. Ask about the last time the person solved that: what happened before, what they tried, what made them give up on the previous alternative. That account reveals what they fired and why, which is the richest information there is for whoever wants to take its place.

A calibration warning: JTBD is a lens, not an oracle. It helps you see competitors outside your category and avoid features nobody would hire, but it does not prioritize alone, does not measure outcomes, and does not dispense with usage data.

# Persona is a communication tool

Segment and persona solve different problems. A SEGMENT is a market slice with similar behavior and needs: 'merchants with up to five orders a day', 'customers who only use the app to pay bills'. It serves to decide where to invest and how to measure. A PERSONA is the representation of a typical person in that group, with a name, context, goal, and barrier, and serves to align the team around whoever is on the other side.

Note the verb: a persona ALIGNS. It does not replace data, proves nothing, and decides nothing alone. It exists so that when someone says 'Renata from the corner store will not understand this field', everyone knows who that is and why.

The problem is that the persona became a decorative deliverable on many teams: a stock photo, an age, an inspiring phrase, and three hobbies. That poster changes no decision, which is why it ends up on the wall with nobody ever looking again. A useful persona has observed behavior, concrete pain, usage context, and a real sentence heard in research.

[["Element","Decorative persona","Useful persona"],["Basis","Team guesswork in one afternoon","Interviews and usage data"],["Content","Age, hobbies, and a nice photo","Behavior, goal, and barrier"],["Quantity","Seven personas for everything","Two or three, revised from time to time"],["Day-to-day use","Stays on the wall slide","Shows up when the team decides something"]]
The test of a persona is simple: has it ever made the team reject an idea? If it never served to say no, it is decoration with a proper name.

## Signs of a useless persona and how to fix it

Three signs give away a dead persona. The first is ORIGIN: born in a two-hour workshop, with no conversation with real people, reflecting what the team imagines about the world. The second is EXCESS: when there are seven personas, none guides decisions, because there is always one that justifies any idea. The third is FREEZING: it was made three years ago, the product changed audience twice, and the poster stays the same.

The fix is cheap. Cut down to two or three, each tied to a segment the business actually serves. Swap hobbies for observable behavior: how often they use it, on what device, what they do when it gets stuck, which alternative they used before. Include the main barrier, the thing keeping the person from getting what they want with your product. And date the document, because personas age too.

Two final cautions. A persona is not a statistical average: describing the average user usually produces someone who does not exist. And a persona is not an excuse to stop doing research; it is the summary of what you have learned so far, not a replacement for learning again.

blocks.value:
# Not all feedback is worth the same

Listening to users is a duty, and listening badly is the most elegant way to build the wrong thing with conviction. Every listening channel carries a built-in bias, and the product person's job is knowing each channel's bias before drawing conclusions.

Whoever complains publicly is a specific sample: usually someone who had a serious problem or is already quite engaged. Whoever answers a survey is someone who had time and an opinion ready. Whoever talks to you at an event is someone engaged enough to be there. None of these groups represents the person who installed the app, understood nothing, and gave up in silence, which is precisely the person with the most to teach.

There is also the VOCAL MINORITY: a small, active, organized group, able to fill the inbox and make the opinion of a few look like consensus. Special care in B2B, where a single big client can turn an internal preference into a roadmap emergency. The question that saves you is always the same: how many people does this represent, and do they look like whom we want to serve?

[["Feedback source","Typical bias","How to compensate"],["App store review","Extremes of rage or passion","Cross with the flow's usage data"],["Form survey","Whoever has time and a ready opinion","Check response rate and profile"],["Support tickets","Only whoever sought help","Look at who gave up without opening a ticket"],["Big B2B client","Commercial weight in the conversation","Check whether the pain shows up across the base"]]
What people say, what they do, and what they say they do are three different things. A serious product checks all three before deciding.

## Saying and doing are not the same thing

The most common example is stated preference. A survey shows most people would love a feature; it launches with fanfare and adoption stays at a few percent. There was no lie: answering a form is cheap, changing behavior is expensive. That is why stated preference alone is worth little, and observed behavior is worth a lot.

The antidote has three parts. First: ask about the PAST, not the future. 'How did you do this last time?' produces information; 'would you use it?' produces politeness. Second: TRIANGULATE. A pain that shows up in interviews, repeats in support tickets, and matches a funnel drop is a real pain; a pain that exists in only one channel is a clue, not a conclusion. Third: look for the SILENCE. Whoever abandoned sign-up will not complain, and that is usually where the biggest available gain lives.

And when the feedback comes with a solution embedded, and it will, keep the problem and discard the solution. 'Put an export button on the home screen' almost always means 'I cannot find my data when I need it'.

lessons.title: Accessibility and inclusion as a product decision

blocks.value:
# Reach, obligation, and opportunity

Accessibility is usually treated as a last-minute technical task, and that is the most expensive reading possible. It is, first of all, a product decision about WHO CAN USE what you build.

It starts with market size. The 2022 Census counted millions of Brazilians with some disability, across visual, hearing, motor, and intellectual. Add TEMPORARY disabilities, like a broken arm or eye surgery, and SITUATIONAL ones, like using the phone in bright sun, with one hand holding a child, or in a loud place with no earphones. The count stops being about a specific group and becomes about practically everyone, at some point.

There is also the regulatory side. The Brazilian Inclusion Law treats digital accessibility as an obligation, not a courtesy, and technical references like the WCAG guidelines guide what to do in practice. In 2026, accessibility requirements already show up often in contracts with public agencies and large companies, which turns the topic into a commercial requirement, not only an ethical one.

[["Barrier","Who it affects","Product decision"],["Low text contrast","Low vision, screen in the sun","Set minimum contrast in design"],["Button with no text label","Screen reader users","Require a label on every element"],["Flow that requires a mouse","Motor disability and keyboard","Guarantee keyboard navigation"],["App too heavy","Old device and limited data","Measure size and load time"]]
Accessibility treated at the end becomes an expensive renovation. Treated at the start, it is almost always a sequence of simple choices nobody notices.

## Inclusion does not stop at disability

In Brazil, the inclusion lens goes further. A good part of many products' base accesses through an entry-level phone, with little memory, on an unstable connection, with a counted data plan. An app that only works well on an expensive phone and fast wi-fi is choosing, without saying so, to serve a narrow slice of the country. Add digital literacy: people new to the internet, older people, those with little formal schooling who do not decode system jargon.

The practical criterion is coming in early and measuring. Accessibility in the team's definition of done, screen-reader and keyboard testing before launch, contrast checked in design, alt text on images that carry information, error messages in plain Portuguese instead of code. None of it is expensive when it is habit; all of it is expensive when it becomes a patch rush after a court notice or a lost contract.

And there is the silent gain: almost every accessibility improvement improves everyone's experience. Good contrast helps whoever is on the bus, a clear label helps whoever is in a hurry, a light app helps even whoever has a new phone.

blocks.value:
# Where the money comes from

Before discussing any feature, it is worth answering one simple, decisive question: how does this product make money? Five models cover most of the market. SUBSCRIPTION: the client pays per period to keep access, as in a management tool or a streaming service; revenue is predictable and the enemy is churn. TRANSACTION: the company keeps a slice of every operation, like a marketplace commission or a payment method's fee; revenue follows the volume flowing through the product. ADS: the advertiser pays and usage is free, so the currency becomes attention and data.

FREEMIUM, strictly speaking, is not a revenue model but an acquisition strategy: a useful free version attracts people and a small slice converts to a paid plan. It works when serving non-payers costs little and when the line between free and paid is honest. LICENSE or one-time sale: you pay once for the right to use it, common in installed corporate software and games.

The point that matters is this: each model rewards a different behavior and, without anyone noticing, shapes the whole product.

[["Model","Who pays","What the product optimizes","Typical risk"],["Subscription","The user, per period","Recurring use and retention","Silent churn"],["Transaction","Whoever operates on the platform","Volume and flow completion","The account only closes at scale"],["Ads","The advertiser","Screen time and reach","User interest takes second place"],["Freemium","A slice of users","Free-to-paid conversion","High cost of serving non-payers"],["License","The client, once","Closing sales and shipping versions","Unpredictable revenue"]]
Tell me how the product makes money and I will tell you what it will prioritize when the goal tightens at quarter end.

## The model shapes the product

Notice how the incentive seeps into decisions. In an ad product, screen time becomes a goal, and that can conflict directly with solving the person's problem quickly. In subscription, the whole team starts living on activation, habit, and a reason to come back, because a client who vanishes for two months cancels in the third. In transaction, availability and flow completion become an obsession: if the operation fails, there is no revenue at that instant. In freemium, deciding what stays free is a product decision, not a sales one. In license, the product lives to justify the next version.

Hybrid models are common: a marketplace with a subscription for sellers plus paid featuring, or a tool with a monthly fee plus usage charges. And switching models means changing the product: starting to charge for something that was free redesigns incentives, communication, and even how teams split.

The health criterion is alignment between what is charged and the value delivered. When revenue grows together with perceived value, product and business push the same way. When it does not, the product that profits while the user wastes time is born, and that contradiction always sends the bill.

blocks.value:
# What it solves, for whom, better than whom

A value proposition is the short answer to a question the market asks all the time: why would I use this, and not the alternative I already have? It has three mandatory parts. WHAT IT SOLVES: the concrete problem, in the language of whoever suffers, not the company's jargon. FOR WHOM: the specific segment, because a proposal that serves everyone convinces no one. BETTER THAN WHOM: the honest comparison with the real alternative.

That third part is the most misjudged. The alternative is almost never the obvious competitor: it is usually the weekend spreadsheet, the improvised group chat, the notebook, the intern doing it by hand, or simply doing nothing and living with the pain. Whoever ignores the real alternative writes a beautiful proposal and loses the sale to Excel.

The fastest quality test: if a competitor could sign your sentence without changing a word, it says nothing. 'We are the complete, innovative platform that simplifies management' describes a thousand companies, so it does not describe yours.

POSITIONING SENTENCE (working draft)

For [specific segment]
who [recurring situation or pain],
[product] is a [known category]
that [main benefit, measurable if possible].
Unlike [the real alternative the person uses today],
it [an advantage the alternative cannot deliver].

Example:
For the small merchant closing the month in a spreadsheet,
X is a payouts dashboard showing how much came in per day
and flagging discrepancies. Unlike the manual spreadsheet,
it reconciles on its own and keeps an auditable history.

[["Part","Question it answers","Common mistake"],["Problem","Which concrete pain goes away?","Describing the feature, not the pain"],["Segment","For whom exactly?","Saying it fits any company"],["Benefit","What improves, and by how much?","Vague adjectives like complete and innovative"],["Alternative","What does the person use today?","Ignoring the spreadsheet and doing nothing"],["Differentiator","Why can't they copy it tomorrow?","Confusing a new feature with an advantage"]]
If your competitor can sign under your value proposition without changing anything, you do not yet have a value proposition.

## A mental canvas, without bureaucracy

There are famous frameworks and canvases for this, and they help. But the essentials fit on one sheet and four questions you answer with evidence, not opinion: whose pain, for whom, compared to what, and why the person would believe you. The belief part is underestimated: a big promise with no proof breeds distrust, and the proof can be a number, a real case, a guarantee, or a friction-free trial.

A value proposition is a HYPOTHESIS until someone demonstrates with behavior that it holds. The ways to test are cheap: present the sentence to ten clients and watch which part makes eyes light up, measure whether a page communicating the proposal converts better than the current one, see how many people follow through when the promise changes.

One final caution for technical teams: a value proposition is not a feature list. 'Integrates with fifteen systems' is a feature; 'you stop typing the same order in two places' is value. Translating between the two is product work, and it is usually the difference between a product that explains itself and one that needs a salesperson for every conversation.

blocks.value:
# CAC, LTV, and margin on a sheet of paper

Unit economics is the math of how much a client is worth and how much it costs to win them. Three numbers are enough to start. CAC (customer acquisition cost) sums everything spent to bring in new clients, including media, commissions, and the sales team, divided by the number of clients who came in. MARGIN is what is left of the price after the cost to serve: infrastructure, payment method fees, support. LTV (customer lifetime value) is how much margin that client leaves while they stay.

The napkin math works like this. A subscription costs 40 reais a month, with a 70% margin, that is, 28 net reais a month. If 5% of the base cancels monthly, the average lifetime is 1 divided by 0.05, that is, 20 months. LTV comes to 28 times 20, or 560 reais. If CAC is 180 reais, the LTV to CAC ratio is about 3.1, and the time to recover the investment is 180 divided by 28, roughly 6 months.

No PM needs to be a financial analyst. You need to be able to do this math in your head.

[["Item","Value in the example","How it is obtained"],["Monthly price","40 reais","Plan charged to the client"],["Monthly margin","28 reais","Price minus cost to serve"],["Monthly churn","5%","Cancellations over the active base"],["Average lifetime","20 months","1 divided by monthly churn"],["LTV","560 reais","Monthly margin times average lifetime"],["CAC","180 reais","Acquisition spend per new client"],["LTV over CAC","3.1","LTV divided by CAC"],["Payback","About 6 months","CAC divided by monthly margin"]]
Retention is not just a product topic, it is the LTV engine. Every churn point shaved extends the client's life and pays for acquisition sooner.

## Where product moves these numbers

Common market references say an LTV to CAC ratio from 3 up and a payback under twelve months indicate a healthy business. They are references, not laws: businesses with expensive capital need shorter paybacks, and long contracts tolerate different numbers. What does not change is the logic: if every client costs more than they return, growing only accelerates the loss.

The product team has direct levers on almost every term. Reducing churn extends average lifetime and inflates LTV. Improving activation gets the client to value before giving up, which shortens payback. Self-service and clear error messages bring down support cost, raising margin. Plan expansion and extra usage raise revenue per client with no new CAC.

Three mistakes always appear. Calculating LTV with gross revenue instead of margin, which produces beautiful, false numbers. Forgetting cost to serve, mainly support and fees. And using very recent cohorts to estimate average lifetime, which always overestimates retention. Simple, honest math beats a sophisticated spreadsheet with the wrong premise.

# Where product grows here

In 2026, four fronts concentrate most product openings in Brazil, and they all share the same origin: large sectors of the economy with still-manual processes.

FINTECH remains the country's biggest product school. The instant payment infrastructure and the financial data sharing rules opened room for a generation of credit, billing, and financial management products for small businesses, and payment methods embedded in other services. HEALTH grows in scheduling, remote care, clinic and plan management, with an important detail: sensitive data and regulation are part of the daily work.

AGRO is the least contested frontier and one of the most interesting: crop management, traceability, input purchasing, and rural credit, with users in the field, unstable connection, and long cycles. EDUCATION stays strong in corporate training, exam prep, and school management. Add retail and logistics, where the fight is last mile, inventory, and the buying experience.

The pattern that matters for a career: the problem is usually more about operations and trust than about cutting-edge technology.

[["Sector","Why product grows there","Common problem type"],["Fintech","New infrastructure and heavy competition","Credit, billing, reconciliation"],["Health","Manual operation and sensitive data","Scheduling, records, adherence"],["Agro","Long chain and little digitization","Crop, traceability, credit"],["Education","Continuous training and scale","Engagement, assessment, management"],["Retail and logistics","Thin margin and high volume","Last mile, inventory, returns"]]
A product opening rarely asks for new technology. It asks for someone who understands the business, reads data without fear, and writes clearly enough to align people.

## What the 2026 openings ask for

Reading product job descriptions in Brazil, five requirements repeat. DATA: querying, reading, and challenging metrics, with basic SQL showing up often even in entry positions. WRITING AND COMMUNICATION: clear documents, decision presentations, alignment with areas that do not report to you. DISCOVERY: talking with users, testing hypotheses, avoiding building what nobody wants. BUSINESS: understanding revenue, cost, and the math sustaining the product. ENGLISH: in a good part of the openings, at least for reading and documentation.

Two practical observations. The first is that an entry opening with the PM title is rare; the door is usually Product Analyst, junior PO, or an internal transition coming from support, data, QA, or development. Working close to product inside the company you are already in is usually the shortest path.

The second is about proof of ability. An isolated certificate impresses little. What changes an interview is being able to tell a complete story: which problem, how you investigated, what you decided, what happened, and what you learned. That holds even when the case is small or came from another role.

# The bridge between the board and the team

There are two metric vocabularies inside the same company, and translating between them is product work. BUSINESS METRICS answer the question 'is the company doing well?': recurring revenue, churn, margin, acquisition cost, satisfaction measured by surveys like NPS. Those are the ones showing up in the results meeting and that the board tracks.

PRODUCT METRICS answer 'is the product delivering value?': how many people reach first value, how long that takes, how often they come back, how many complete the main task without error, how many use the feature that sustains the proposition. Those are metrics the team can move within the week.

The problem starts when someone charges the team with a metric it does not control alone. Revenue depends on price, campaigns, market, and seasonality; a product team influences it but does not determine it. The way out is not fleeing the business number, it is building the bridge: showing which product metric feeds that outcome and taking that one as the operational goal.

[["Business metric","Product metric feeding it","Team lever"],["Recurring revenue","Activation and use of the paid feature","Reduce friction to first value"],["Churn","Usage frequency in the first month","Create a real reason to return"],["Cost to serve","Tickets per active client","Self-service and clearer errors"],["NPS","Success on the main task","Remove friction from the central flow"]]

## NPS, churn, and what they do not say

NPS comes from a single question about the likelihood of recommending, on a zero-to-ten scale. Nine or ten is a promoter, seven and eight are neutral, zero to six are detractors; the index is the percentage of promoters minus detractors, ranging from minus one hundred to one hundred. It is a useful relationship thermometer, and terrible as a compass: it says something is going well or badly, never what to do. The real value is in the open comment field after the score, and in comparing your own series over time, not with another company's number.

Churn also deceives when looked at as a single number. There is VOLUNTARY churn, when the person decides to leave, and INVOLUNTARY, when payment fails due to an expired card or limit. The second usually accounts for a relevant slice and is solved with product and communication, not a new feature.

The practice sustaining the bridge is the metric tree: write the business outcome at the top, break it into the behaviors producing it, and pick one as the quarter's focus. Whoever sees that path can defend priority with a business argument, which is the conversation that opens doors in a career.

# Writing is product's main tool

Whoever works in product writes all day: problem documents, decision summaries, messages aligning three areas, release notes. It is not bureaucracy, it is the craft's central tool, for two reasons.

The first is that WRITING EXPOSES HOLES IN REASONING. In conversation, you can hold up a loose idea with tone, gestures, and charm. In text, no. When you try to write why that problem is a priority and get stuck on the third line, you just discovered you do not yet understand the problem. That discomfort is the exercise's biggest benefit, not a side effect.

The second is that TEXT SCALES. A meeting aligns whoever was in the room at that hour; a document aligns whoever arrived later, whoever was on vacation, whoever joined the team next month, and the area only affected next quarter. Product lives on shared context, and context that exists only in participants' memory vanishes fast.

The most useful format for decisions is the ONE-PAGE document. It forces you to choose what matters and fits in the decider's calendar.

PRODUCT ONE PAGER (one page, no mandatory attachment)

Problem: who suffers, in what situation, how often, at what cost
Evidence: 3 facts with source and date (usage, tickets, interviews)
Goal: which outcome we want to move and in what time frame
Options considered: A, B, and doing nothing, with cost and risk
Recommendation: which option and why, in one sentence
How we will know: success metric and when we will read it
Risks: what could go wrong and what would change our mind
Decision requested: what you need from whoever is reading

[["Document","When to use","Target size"],["One pager","Asking for a decision","One page, no attachment"],["Decision record","After deciding something","A few paragraphs with a date"],["Problem document","Before discussing solution","One to two pages"],["Release note","Communicating what changed","Short, with explicit impact"]]
If you cannot write the decision on one page, you have not decided yet. You are negotiating with your own doubt using slides as anesthesia.

## Six rules that improve any product text

First: START WITH THE CONCLUSION. Readers want to know right away what you are proposing and what needs an answer; the reasoning comes after, for whoever wants to check it. Second: one document, one subject. A text handling three decisions gets none.

Third: data with SOURCE AND DATE. 'Conversion fell' supports nothing; 'sign-up conversion fell from 42% to 31% between March and May, measured on the funnel dashboard' supports. Fourth: write for whoever arrives with no context, because that person always shows up, and is usually the one deciding.

Fifth: cut jargon and adjectives. 'Robust and scalable solution' informs nothing; 'handles the Monday peak with no queue' informs. Sixth: revise by cutting. Almost every first draft shrinks twenty percent losing nothing, and gets stronger.

One habit that changes a beginner's career: after any relevant decision, write five lines with what was decided, why, who decided, and what was discarded. In three months, you will have a history answering 'why did we do it this way?' without depending on anyone's memory, and you become the team's natural reference.

# Context, options, recommendation

There is a format that solves most product presentations, and it has three parts. CONTEXT: what the problem is, why now, what we already know. OPTIONS: the paths considered, with cost, risk, and what each sacrifices, always including the option of doing nothing. RECOMMENDATION: which you would pick, why, and what would make you change your mind.

The third part is what separates a professional from a messenger. Presenting three options without recommending transfers the decision to the audience and doubles the meeting's length. Recommending without showing the alternatives sounds like imposition and invites the audience to invent options mid-conversation. Both together produce the effect you want: listeners understand the reasoning, trust the process, and decide fast.

An underestimated detail: say from the start WHAT YOU NEED from that room. A decision? Budget approval? Just information? A meeting with no explicit ask ends in 'cool, let's think about it', and returns to the calendar two weeks later with the same topic and less energy.

[["Part","What goes in","Common mistake"],["Context","Problem, urgency, and evidence","Telling the project's whole story"],["Options","Paths with cost and risk","Hiding the uncomfortable alternative"],["Recommendation","Your pick and the why","Not recommending out of fear"],["Ask","What you need from the room","Ending without defining the next step"]]
A decision meeting that ends without a decision becomes another meeting, with the same people, less energy, and the problem slightly more expensive.

## How to run the conversation

Send the material beforehand, and make clear the pre-read is expected. It saves half the meeting and improves the questions. Open by stating the ask in one sentence: 'I need the decision between A and B today, because the integration window closes on the twentieth'. Then present context and options without dressing up the path you prefer: whoever notices only your option was well described loses trust in the rest.

When there is disagreement, separate the TYPE OF DISAGREEMENT. If it is about fact, it resolves with data, and sometimes getting the data later beats arguing in the dark. If it is about tolerated risk, it belongs to whoever answers for the outcome. If it is about priority, the conversation is strategy, not solution, and maybe the meeting changes subject.

Always close with a record: what was decided, who decided, what is pending, who does what by when. Publish the same day. A decision that does not become text disappears, and you will spend the same energy a month from now defending something that was already agreed.
