lessons.title: Saying no with evidence and an alternative

blocks.value:
# No is part of the work

Prioritizing is choosing, and choosing means saying no to legitimate things, requested by reasonable people, that would solve real problems. Whoever cannot say no ends up saying yes to everything, and the result is worse for everyone: the team carries thirty items in progress, nothing finishes on time, and trust wears down in silence. The cowardly yes is more destructive than the clear no.

There are three different noes, and confusing them creates unnecessary fights. 'NOT NOW' acknowledges the value and explains the queue: something else is ahead by a criterion, and there is a scheduled moment to revisit. 'NOT THIS WAY' accepts the problem and refuses the proposed solution, offering a cheaper or safer path. And 'NO, BECAUSE IT CONFLICTS' is the hardest: it goes against the period's goal or the audience we chose to serve, and it is not a matter of queue.

All three only work with two things attached: EVIDENCE of why the priority is elsewhere and an ALTERNATIVE for what can be done instead, even if small.

[["Type of no","When to use","What must come with it"],["Not now","The value exists, the queue is elsewhere","The queue's criterion and review date"],["Not this way","The problem is real, the solution is not","A cheaper alternative path"],["No, it conflicts","It goes against the period's goal","The goal and whoever set it"],["Cowardly yes","Never","Nothing: it only postpones frustration"]]
A no with an explained criterion earns respect. A yes that never happens breeds distrust, and you pay that bill in the next negotiation.

## How to say no without burning the relationship

The sequence that works has four steps. First, REPEAT THE PROBLEM in the requester's own words, until the person agrees you understood. Much of the conflict is born from not feeling heard, not from the refusal itself. Second, show the queue and the criterion: what is ahead, for what reason, and the expected outcome. Transparency about the criterion turns a personal decision into a product decision.

Third, offer something: a minimal version that fits now, a temporary operational workaround, a date to revisit with new data, or the commitment to measure the pain to decide better next cycle. Fourth, record it in writing, with a date. It protects both sides and avoids the eternal reopening of the same topic.

And there is the no you should not give alone. When the request carries legal risk, a signed contractual commitment, or serious business consequence, the decision needs to go up with clarity, and that is not weakness: it is recognizing who answers for what. Escalating well means bringing context, options, and a recommendation, not pushing the problem upstairs.

# Who they are and what each one wants

A stakeholder is anyone who affects your product or is affected by it. The list is longer than it seems: board, sales, marketing, support, operations, finance, legal, compliance, information security, partners, and, in regulated sectors, even the supervisory agency. Each arrives with their own goal, and it is almost never yours.

Understanding the other's goal is the shortcut to stop treating stakeholders as obstacles. Sales wants to close a contract this month, and that is why they ask for the feature that unblocks the current client. Support wants to reduce ticket volume and suffers from the problem nobody prioritizes. Legal wants low risk, and that is why they block what seemed simple. None of them is a villain; all answer to goals the company created.

The PM who sees this changes the conversation: instead of 'no can do', they can say 'I understand you need to close the contract; is there a path that solves it in two weeks without breaking the roadmap?'. The negotiation becomes about GOALS, not personal wills.

[["Quadrant","Recommended stance","Conversation cadence","Typical example"],["High influence, high interest","Involve in the decision","Talk before deciding"],["High influence, low interest","Keep satisfied","Short summary, no surprises"],["Low influence, high interest","Keep informed","Regular written updates"],["Low influence, low interest","Monitor","Only when the topic touches them"]]
No surprises in the meeting. If someone important will disagree with your proposal, it is better to discover that the day before, in a one-on-one.

## A simple map that avoids many crises

The classic map crosses two questions: how much does this person care about the topic, and how much can they influence the outcome. It needs no tool: a sheet split into four quadrants does it. The value is not the drawing, it is the discipline of asking two questions before every big decision: who is affected by this, and who can block this?

From there, behavior changes. With whoever has high influence and high interest, you talk BEFORE, with the proposal still in draft, because that person needs to feel part of the decision. With whoever has high influence and little interest, you send a short summary and avoid taking their time: that person just does not want surprises. With whoever has high interest and little influence, like support and operations, you inform regularly, because they carry the day-to-day impact.

Two final reminders. The map changes with every reorg, goal shift, or leadership change, so revise it. And a difficult stakeholder is, in the vast majority of cases, someone with a goal misaligned with yours, not someone acting in bad faith. Finding out what that goal is usually solves more than any negotiation technique.

# Writing to be read later

Distributed teams permanently changed product communication. In 2026, it is common for one team to have people in different time zones, with different routines, and information must work without everyone being online at the same time. The central skill becomes writing for whoever will read LATER, without you around to explain.

That changes the message's shape. Synchronous communication tolerates incomplete context because the other person asks right away. Async does not: a message that generates three questions back costs a full day of waiting. So the rule is delivering the complete package: what happened, why it matters, what you propose, what you need from the person, and by when.

The cost of meetings becomes more visible in this setup. Eight people for one hour consume a combined workday. That does not mean abolishing meetings: it means reserving them for what truly requires real time, like hard negotiation, delicate conversations, alignment with much ambiguity, and moments of joint building. The rest becomes text.

[["Situation","Right channel","Why"],["Aligning a decision with trade-offs","Document and comments","Everyone reads and responds calmly"],["Hard negotiation","Live conversation","Tone and reaction matter a lot"],["Work status","Board or written summary","Nobody needs a meeting for this"],["Quick team question","Team message channel","Short answer, visible to all"],["Personal feedback","Live, private conversation","Text hardens what is sensitive"]]
Eight people in a one-hour meeting cost a full day of work. If the outcome fits in a document, you just spent a day for nothing.

## Rules that sustain an async team

First: every kind of information has ONE known place. Decisions live in the decision log, requirements in the work item, discussion in the document, announcements in the team channel. When important information lives in two people's private chat, the whole team depends on someone else's memory.

Second: a message asking for something states the DEADLINE and the TYPE of response expected. 'I need your OK by Thursday, or a comment on what blocks it' works; 'what do you think?' goes unanswered for a week. Third: publish decisions the same day, even short ones, and always in the agreed place.

Fourth: respect time zones and routines. Demanding immediate replies in a distributed team destroys the model's main gain, which is the ability to work with focus. Fifth: visibility is not surveillance. A weekly summary of what advanced, what is stuck, and what comes next reassures stakeholders and replaces the temptation of micromanagement.

The good side effect is that mature async teams write better, decide with more informed people, and suffer less when any specific person is away.

lessons.title: Picking the target and the method

blocks.value:
# Analyzing a product from the outside, with method

A TEARDOWN is the structured analysis of a product you did not build, done only with what you can observe from outside. It is the cheapest exercise there is to train a product eye: no access needed, no permission needed, and it forces you to practice everything you have seen so far on a concrete case.

The target choice matters more than it seems. Prefer a product you USE SOMEWHAT OFTEN, because you already know the flow, and that is not an object of passion, because a fan does not see friction. Also prefer a product with a broad audience, which makes the segment easier to understand, and avoid internal company tools, whose context you cannot reconstruct from outside.

Scope is the second decision. Analyzing 'the whole app' produces generic text. Pick ONE MAIN FLOW, like first purchase, first account creation, search to result, or plan renewal, and go deep on it. Set aside three to five hours, split into at least two sessions, with a gap between them. Distance helps separate fact from momentary irritation.

TEARDOWN SCRIPT (3 to 5 hours, in two sessions)

1. Target and scope: which product, which flow, on what device
2. Value proposition: what it promises, for whom, against which alternative
3. Likely users: visible segments and each one's main job
4. Revenue model: who pays, for what, what is free and why
5. Journey: from first contact to first value, counting steps
6. Metrics: likely north star and likely funnel, always as hypotheses
7. Strategy: real competitors, differentiator, and what sustains it
8. What I would do: 3 bets with expected metric and each one's risk
9. Limits: what cannot be known looking from outside

[["Target type","Why it works well","Caution"],["Delivery or ride app","Short flow, broad audience","Many people already analyzed the obvious"],["Digital bank or wallet","Rich, regulated onboarding","External rules explain a lot"],["Niche marketplace","Two sides visible in the interface","You only see one side"],["Work tool","Clear job, obvious alternative","The buyer is not the user"]]
You are analyzing from outside, with public information. Every conclusion about someone else's intent is a hypothesis, and writing that with honesty is what separates analysis from guessing.

## The method, step by step

The sequence that works has four separate stages, and mixing them is the most common mistake. USE: walk the flow as if it were your first time, noting nothing, paying attention to what you feel. RECORD: redo the same path noting observable facts, steps, screens, texts, and points where you hesitated. ANALYZE: only afterwards, away from the app, apply the script's questions. WRITE: assemble the final document with hypotheses clearly labeled.

Three honesty rules sustain the work. First: SEPARATE OBSERVATION FROM INTERPRETATION. 'The checkout button only appears after scrolling' is an observation; 'maybe that is why many people abandon' is an interpretation. Second: assert nothing about what happens inside the company, internal numbers, or the real reason for a decision. You do not know, and a good teardown says so out loud.

Third: critique the product, never the people. And date the document, because products change: an undated analysis ages badly and becomes a source of wrong information six months later.

# From first contact to first value

The teardown's heart is the journey, and it starts before the app: in the store, on the website, in the ad promising something. Note the PROMISE that brought the person there, because every following friction will be judged against it.

Then comes ONBOARDING, the stretch between first contact and the moment the person receives something of value. Record precisely: how many screens, how many fields, how many permissions requested, how long until the first real value. Pay special attention to what is DEMANDED BEFORE DELIVERING: asking for full sign-up, documents, and location permission before showing any benefit is a product decision with a high cost, and sometimes a good reason behind it, like a regulatory requirement.

Next, the MAIN JOB: the task the person is there for. Walk that path counting steps and taps, and mark every point where you hesitated, went back, reread, or erred. Hesitation is the exercise's most valuable data, because it is the visible trail of a doubt many other people also had.

[["Stage","What to record","Analyst's question"],["Initial promise","Store and ad copy","Does the product deliver what it promised?"],["Onboarding","Screens, fields, permissions","What is asked before delivering value?"],["First value","Time and steps to get there","Can this path be shortened?"],["Main job","Taps, errors, hesitations","Where does the person likely give up?"],["Return","Reason to come back tomorrow","What brings the person back?"]]
Take notes as an analyst, not as a fan or an irritated critic. What matters is not whether you liked it, but what the interface asks, delivers, and hides.

## How to record without fooling yourself

Use simple, disciplined instruments. Count STEPS and taps to the goal, time the TIME TO FIRST VALUE, capture the screens where something blocked you, and write one line next to each capture saying what happened there. Approximate numbers serve: seven taps and two minutes is information; 'it felt slow' is not.

The technique that most improves the result is observing ANOTHER PERSON. Ask someone who has never used the product to do a simple task, warn them you cannot help, and stay quiet, taking notes. It will hurt to watch the person miss the obvious button, and that is exactly the discomfort that teaches. Five minutes of this reveals more than an hour of your own opinion.

Finally, split your notes into three columns: OBSERVATION, INTERPRETATION, and OPINION. The first is what anyone would see; the second is your reading of why; the third is personal taste, and it can stay out of the final document. Whole teams lose credibility mixing the three in a single paragraph, and you do not need to repeat that mistake in your first public material.

# What this product probably measures

You have no access to anyone's dashboard, and that is exactly why this exercise is good: it forces reasoning from public evidence. The interface reveals priority. What the product puts on the home screen, what it highlights with color, what it pushes by notification, what the pricing page charges, and what the campaign promises are clues to what that team is trying to move.

The most useful concept here is the NORTH STAR: a metric representing the value delivered to the user which, when it grows healthily, tends to pull the business along. A good candidate meets three criteria. First, it measures value received, not company effort. Second, the team can influence it with its own work. Third, there is an explainable path between it and revenue.

That is why downloads, sign-ups, and likes rarely work: they are vanity metrics, they rise with campaigns and say nothing about whether anyone received value. Better formats usually involve frequency, completion, or the quantity of something successfully delivered, like completed orders per active client per month.

[["Product type","Plausible north star","Likely funnel"],["Delivery","Completed orders per active client","Open, search, build cart, pay"],["Streaming","Hours watched per active subscriber","Enter, choose, start, finish"],["Marketplace","Deals closed between both sides","Search, compare, negotiate, pay"],["Work tool","Tasks completed per active team","Create account, configure, invite, use"]]
Downloads rise with campaigns and fall with forgetting. A good metric is one that only grows when someone on the other side received real value.

## Writing metrics as a testable hypothesis

The format that gives the exercise seriousness is this: 'HYPOTHESIS: this product's north star is X. PUBLIC EVIDENCE: the home screen highlights X, notifications push X, and the paid plan charges by X. HOW I WOULD CHECK WITH ACCESS: I would look at X's series per cohort and the relation between X and renewal'. Three sentences, and the analysis stops being a guess.

Also draw the LIKELY FUNNEL, that is, the stages to value: arrive, understand, do the minimum setup, complete the task once, come back. For each stage, point out where the interface seems to protect the passage, with a shortcut, a pre-filled default, a reminder, or an incentive. Where there is heavy retention effort, there is usually a known drop.

Do not forget the COUNTER-METRIC, the number preventing dumb optimization. A product chasing screen time must watch cancellations and complaints; one chasing conversion must watch regret, returns, and support tickets. Pointing out the counter-metric in a teardown shows maturity, because it reveals you understand that any isolated metric can be gamed by a well-intentioned team under pressure.

# Competitors, differentiator, and bets

The strategy part of a teardown starts with a simple, badly answered question: who does this product really compete against? The answer is rarely the list of companies in the same category. A personal finance app competes with the spreadsheet, the notebook, and the habit of not looking at the account. A management tool competes with the group chat that already works badly, but works. A competitor is anything that does the same job in the person's life.

Then comes the DIFFERENTIATOR, and here the criterion is defensibility. A beautiful feature is copyable in one quarter. Hard to copy is something else: network effects, when the product improves as more people join; high switching costs, when leaving hurts because of history, integrations, or process; structural cost advantage; brand and trust built over years; and access to data that only accumulated usage generates.

When you find none of those, the honest hypothesis is that the product competes on execution and speed, which is legitimate and fragile at the same time.

[["Differentiator","What sustains it","How it weakens"],["Network effect","Each new user adds value","The audience migrates in bulk elsewhere"],["Switching cost","History, integration, process","A competitor makes import easy"],["Brand and trust","Years of consistent delivery","One badly handled serious episode"],["Cost advantage","Scale and lean operation","A new entrant with a smaller structure"],["Accumulated data","Usage that improves the service","New rules about data use"]]
Before saying what you would do differently, write what you cannot see from outside: contracts, regulation, technical debt, and data that contradict your intuition.

## What I would do differently, and why

This is the section that most reveals professional level, and also the one that most ruins amateur teardowns. The classic mistake is the list of loose guesses: 'a bigger button', 'a different color', 'add artificial intelligence'. Nothing there is discussable, because nothing is tied to a problem, expected outcome, or risk.

The format that works turns each suggestion into a written BET. Start with the observed problem, with the public evidence supporting it. Describe the proposed change in one sentence. Say which metric should move and in which direction. Point out the counter-metric you would watch. And finish with the cheapest test able to indicate whether the bet pays, because proposing an experiment is stronger than proposing certainty.

Two or three well-written bets beat fifteen suggestions. And keep the humility explicit: you cannot see contracts, regulatory obligations, inherited constraints, or the results of tests the team already ran and discarded. Writing 'if there is no constraint I cannot see' does not weaken the analysis; on the contrary, it is what makes an experienced person take your text seriously.

# From isolated exercise to portfolio piece

A teardown done and filed away trains the eye. A teardown published becomes proof of reasoning, and proof of reasoning is what opens doors for whoever does not yet have a product title on their badge. The difference between the two is only the final organization.

The format that works fits in two pages. Start with the SUMMARY: which product, which flow, when it was done, and the three main conclusions. Then the analysis, following the script you already used: value proposition, users and job, revenue model, journey with observed numbers, metric and strategy hypotheses. Finish with the written bets, the analysis's limits, and what would change your mind with more information.

Two form choices make a difference. Label EVERY hypothesis as a hypothesis, without exception, and avoid any claim about what happens inside the company. And date the document, because products change and an old undated analysis ages badly. An honest teardown of a simple product beats an ambitious text full of conclusions you cannot support.

The habit matters more than the single piece. Whoever analyzes one product a month for a year sees patterns no course can teach in one class.

## The mental map you take from here

It is worth tying together what this journey built, because everything was used in the teardown. Product is not project: it evolves as long as the problem exists, and the scoreboard is OUTCOME, not output. Each lifecycle phase asks for a different game, and each product type, from B2C to platform, changes the decider's tools.

The roles exist without myth: the PM owns the problem, PO and Analyst are legitimate entry doors, and the title matters less than the real scope. The work happens on a team, with the trio deciding together, rituals that must justify themselves, engineering treated as a business partner, and design as an investigation partner.

The user enters through the problem, not the enchanting solution; the job explains choices demographics do not; feedback demands methodical distrust; and accessibility is a decision about reach. The business sustains itself on a revenue model, a value proposition, and a napkin math everyone should be able to do. And all of it only becomes a decision when someone writes clearly, presents options, says no with criteria, and keeps the right people informed.

Pick the next product, block the hours on your calendar, and do it again. That is how fundamentals become a trained eye.
